==English== ===Etymology 1=== {{root|en|ine-pro|*preyH-}} From {{inh|en|enm|appropriaten}}, from {{af|enm|appropriat|-en|t1=appropriated|id2=infinitival|nocat=1}}, borrowed from {{der|en|la|appropriātus}}, {{glossary|perfect}} {{glossary|passive}} {{glossary|participle}} of {{m|la|appropriō||to make one's own}}, from {{m|la|ad||to}} + {{m|la|propriō||to make one's own}}, from {{af|la|proprius|-ō|t1=one's own, private|pos2=first conjugation verb-forming suffix|id2=denominative|nocat=1}}. ====Pronunciation==== * {{IPA|en|/əˈpɹəʊ.pɹi.eɪt/|a=RP}} * {{IPA|en|/əˈpɹoʊ.pɹi.eɪt/|a=GA}} ** {{audio|en|en-us-appropriate-verb.ogg|a=US}} ====Verb==== {{en-verb}} # {{lb|en|transitive}} To take to oneself; to claim or use, especially as by an exclusive right. #: {{ux|en|Let no man '''appropriate''' the use of a common benefit.}} #* {{RQ:Landon Ethel Churchill|page=179|volume=II|passage="I promise you," said she, after a pause of some minutes, "to wear the last new dress you gave me, it is a triumph of taste!"
Lord Marchmont bowed, and '''appropriated''' the compliment as if the taste had been his own, not the milliner's.}} #* {{RQ:Churchill Celebrity|chapter=5|passage=We made an odd party before the arrival of the Ten, particularly when the Celebrity dropped in for lunch or dinner. He could not be induced to remain permanently at Mohair because Miss Trevor was at Asquith, but he '''appropriated''' a Hempstead cart from the Mohair stables and made the trip sometimes twice in a day.}} #* {{quote-journal|en|year=1962|month=December|title=Motive Power Miscellany: North Eastern Region|journal=Modern Railways|pages=422, 425|text=On the morning after the one-day strike, October 4, one of the Type 4s on crew-training, No. D169, was '''appropriated''' to head the 3 a.m. mail to Hull, as no steam locomotive had been lit up and the usual Hull Type 3 was not available; [...].}} # {{lb|en|transitive}} To set apart for, or assign to, a particular person or use, especially in exclusion of all others; with ''to'' or ''for''. #: {{ux|en|A spot of ground is '''appropriated''' for a garden.}} #: {{co|en|to '''appropriate''' money for the increase of the navy}} # {{lb|en|transitive|British|ecclesiastical|legal}} To [[annex]] (for example a [[benefice]], to a [[spiritual]] [[corporation]], as its [[property]]). #* {{quote-book|en|year=1793|author=w:Edward Christian|chapter=Of the Clergy|mainauthor=w:William Blackstone; Edward Christian|title={{w|Commentaries on the Laws of England}},{{nb...|in Four Books. By Sir William Blackstone, Knt., One of the Justices of His Majesty’s Court of Common Pleas. The Twelfth Edition, with the Last Corrections of the Author; and with Notes and Additions by Edward Christian, Esq., Barrister at Law, and Professor of the Laws of England in the University of Cambridge.}}|edition=12th|volume_plain=book I (Of the Rights of Persons)|location=London|publisher={{...|Printed by}} [[w:Andrew Strahan|A{{quote-gloss|ndrew}} Strahan]] and [[w:William Woodfall|W{{quote-gloss|illiam}} Woodfall]], {{...|law-printers to the King’s Most Excellent Majesty,}} for [[w:Thomas Cadell (publisher)|T{{quote-gloss|homas}} Cadell]],{{nb...|in the Strand.}}|section=note 23|pages=387–388|pageurl=https://archive.org/details/bim_eighteenth-century_commentaries-on-the-laws_blackstone-william-sir_1793_1/page/n533/mode/1up|oclc=3462973|passage=A vicar, from what has been advanced in the preceding page and note, muſt neceſſarily have an appropriator over him, or a ſinecure rector, who in ſome books is conſidered and called an appropriator. Of benefices, ſome have never been '''appropriated'''; conſequently in thoſe there there can be no vicar, and the incumbent is rector, and entitled to all the dues of the church. Some were '''appropriated''' to ſecular eccleſiaſtical corporations, which appropriations ſtill exiſt, except perhaps ſome few which may have been diſſolved; others were '''appropriated''' to the houſes of the regular clergy; all which appropriations, at the diſſolution of monaſteries, were transferred to the crown; and in the hands of the king or his grantees are now called impropriations: but in ſome '''appropriated''' churches no perpetual vicar has ever been endowed; in that caſe the officiating miniſter is appointed by the appropriator or impropriator, and is called a perpetual curate.}} # {{lb|en|transitive|archaic}} To make suitable {{m|en|to}}; to [[suit]]. #* {{quote-book|en|year=1790|author=w:Helen Maria Williams|title=Julia|page=67|publisher=Routledge|year_published=2016 |passage=Under the towers were a number of gloomy subterraneous apartments with vaulted roofs, the use of which imagination was left to guess, and could only '''appropriate''' to punishment and horror.}} #* {{quote-book|en|year=1802|author=w:William Paley|title= Natural Theology or Evidences of the Existence and Attributes of the Deity |passage=Were we to take a portion of the skin, and contemplate its exquisite sensibility, so finely '''appropriated''' {{...}} we should have no occasion to draw our argument, for the twentieth time, from the structure of the eye or the ear.}} #* {{quote-book|en|year=1927|title=Plain Talk|page=94 |passage=The fellow across the road gives up farming and turns his place into a pastoral bootleggery . Picnickers '''appropriate''' the lawn and declare for the proletariat . The sheriff comes , argues with them and they depart , leaving the Sunday [...]}} =====Synonyms===== * {{sense|to take to oneself}} {{l|en|help oneself}}, {{l|en|impropriate}}; see also [[Thesaurus:take]] or [[Thesaurus:steal]] * {{sense|to set apart for}} {{l|en|allocate}}, {{l|en|earmark}}; see also [[Thesaurus:set apart]] =====Derived terms===== {{col3|en|reappropriate|appropriater|appropriable|appropriatory|appropriative|appropriator|disappropriate|malappropriate|misappropriate|unappropriate}} =====Translations===== {{trans-top|to take to oneself in exclusion of others}} * Azerbaijani: * Bulgarian: * Chinese: * Czech: * Danish: * Dutch: * Esperanto: * Finnish: * Galician: * Georgian: * German: * Gothic: * Hebrew: * Hungarian: * Japanese: * Māori: * Norwegian: * Old English: * Polish: * Portuguese: * Romanian: * Russian: {{t+|ru|присва́ивать|impf}}, {{t+|ru|присво́ить|pf}} * Slovene: * Spanish: * Swedish: * Ukrainian: {{trans-bottom}} {{trans-top-see|to set apart for|designate}} * Bulgarian: * Czech: * Dutch: * Finnish: * German: * Hungarian: * Japanese: * Portuguese: * Russian: {{t+|ru|ассигнова́ть|impf|pf}}; {{t+|ru|выделя́ть|impf}}, {{t+|ru|вы́делить|pf}} * Slovene: * Ukrainian: {{trans-bottom}} {{trans-top|law: to annex}} * Finnish: * German: * Hungarian: * Norwegian: * Old English: * Swedish: {{trans-bottom}} {{trans-top|to make suitable}} * Czech: * Danish: * Dutch: * Esperanto: * Finnish: * French: * German: * Hungarian: * Norwegian: * Portuguese: * Romanian: * Russian: {{t+|ru|приспосо́бить|pf}}, {{t+|ru|приспособля́ть|impf}}, {{t+|ru|приспоса́бливать|impf}} * Swedish: {{trans-bottom}} ===Etymology 2=== From {{inh|en|enm|appropriat||appropriated}}, see {{af|en|-ate|id1=adjective|pos1=adjective-forming suffix}} and [[#Etymology 1|Etymology 1]] for more. ====Pronunciation==== * {{enPR|əprō'priĭt|əprō'priət|a=RP}}, {{IPA|en|/əˈpɹəʊ.pɹi.ɪt/|/-ət/}} * {{enPR|əprō'priĭt|əprō'priət|a=GA}}, {{IPA|en|/əˈpɹoʊ.pɹi.ɪt/|/-ət/}} * {{audio|en|en-us-appropriate-adj.ogg|a=US}} ====Adjective==== {{en-adj}} # [[suitable|Suitable]] or [[fit]]; [[proper]]; [[felicitous]]. #: {{ux|en|The headmaster wondered what an '''appropriate''' measure would be to make the pupil behave better.}} #* '''1798-1801''', {{w|Beilby Porteus}}, ''Lecture XI delivered in the Parish Church of St. James, Westminster'' #* {{quote-book|en|year=1710|author=w:Edward Stillingfleet|title=Several Conferences Between a Romish Priest, a Fanatick Chaplain, and a Divine of the Church of England Concerning the Idolatry of the Church of Rome |passage='''appropriate''' acts of divine worship}} # Suitable to the social situation or to social respect or social discreetness; [[socially]] [[correct]]; [[socially]] [[discreet]]; [[well-mannered]]; [[proper]]. #: {{ux|en|I don't think it was '''appropriate''' for the cashier to tell me out loud in front of all those people at the checkout that my hairpiece looked like it was falling out of place.}} #: {{ux|en|While it is not considered '''appropriate''' for a professor to date his student, there is no such concern once the semester has ended.}} #* {{RQ:Telegraph|date=November 10, 2011 |author=Jeremy Wilson |title=England Under 21 5 Iceland Under 21 0: match report |url=http://www.telegraph.co.uk/sport/football/teams/england/8882713/England-Under-21-5-Iceland-Under-21-0-match-report.html |passage=With such focus from within the footballing community this week on Remembrance Sunday, there was something '''appropriate''' about Colchester being the venue for last night’s game. Troops from the garrison town formed a guard of honour for both sets of players, who emerged for the national anthem with poppies proudly stitched into their tracksuit jackets.|archiveurl=https://web.archive.org/web/20251104215249/https://www.telegraph.co.uk/sport/football/teams/england/8882713/England-Under-21-5-Iceland-Under-21-0-match-report.html|archivedate=4 November 2025}} # {{lb|en|obsolete}} Set apart for a particular use or person; [[reserved]]. # Of an action or thing: [[morally]] [[good]]; [[positive]]. #: {{ux|en|Rescuing animals is an '''appropriate''' thing to do.}} # Of an action or thing: [[pleasant]]. =====Synonyms===== * {{sense|suited for}} {{l|en|apt}}, {{l|en|felicitous}}, {{l|en|fitting}}, {{l|en|suitable}}; see also [[Thesaurus:suitable]] =====Antonyms===== * {{antsense|all senses}} {{l|en|inappropriate}} * {{l|en|unhappy}} =====Derived terms===== {{col|en|appropes|appropriately|nonappropriate|unappropriate|appropriateness}} {{col4|en|title=Compound words and expressions |age-appropriate |appropriate adult |appropriate technology |culturally appropriate }} =====Related terms===== {{col4|en |appropriation |proper |property }} =====Translations===== {{trans-top-see|peculiar, suitable, fit, proper|adequate}} * Albanian: * Arabic: * Armenian: * Azerbaijani: * Basque: * Belarusian: * Bulgarian: * Catalan: * Chinese: * Czech: * Danish: * Dutch: * Esperanto: * Estonian: * Finnish: * French: * Galician: * Georgian: * German: * Greek: * Hebrew: * Hiligaynon: * Hindi: * Hungarian: * Icelandic: * Indonesian: * Irish: * Italian: * Japanese: * Khmer: * Korean: * Latin: * Latvian: * Malay: * Māori: * Middle English: * Norwegian: * Old Norse: * Polish: * Portuguese: * Romanian: * Russian: {{t+|ru|соотве́тствующий}}, {{t+|ru|подходя́щий}} * Scottish Gaelic: * Serbo-Croatian: * Slovene: * Spanish: * Swahili: * Swedish: * Thai: * Turkish: * Ukrainian: * Vietnamese: * Welsh: * Yiddish: {{trans-bottom}} {{trans-top|suitable to social situation}} * Arabic: * Armenian: * Czech: * Danish: * Dutch: * Finnish: * Galician: * German: * Hindi: * Hungarian: * Māori: * Middle English: * Norwegian: * Polish: * Portuguese: * Romanian: * Russian: {{t+|ru|уме́стный}}, {{t+|ru|подходя́щий}} * Scottish Gaelic: * Serbo-Croatian: * Slovene: * Swedish: * Turkish: * Welsh: * Yiddish: {{trans-bottom}} {{trans-top|obsolete: set apart for a particular use or person}} * Dutch: * Finnish: * Galician: * German: * Italian: * Portuguese: * Romanian: * Spanish: * Turkish: {{trans-bottom}} ===Further reading=== * {{R:OneLook}} * {{R:Webster 1913}} {{cln|en|heteronyms}}
